subsubtopic: PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF QUESTIONING OF FOUR CANADIANS BY RUSSIAN AGENTS IN CUBA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity arising from information given the House by the government yesterday which appears contrary to the facts concerning the holding in custody and questioning of four Canadian citizens by allegedly Russian KGB agents after they made a forced landing by air in Cuba on December 30. I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
That in view of the statements by pilot Robert Carter that his group received no assistance from the Department of External Affairs while held in Cuba and that he was not contacted immediately on their return to Canada by Canadian officials, the House requests a full investigation and statement on the facts of this matter by the Secretary of State for External Affairs; and further, the House instructs the Prime Minister during his current stay in Havana to make representations to Prime Minister Castro in regard to this unwarranted and unlawful holding of Canadian citizens on Cuban soil by Russian KGB agents and that he advise Mr. Castro that Canada is not prepared to tolerate further incidents of this kind.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member talks about the reaction of the U.S. government I am not sure whether he is referring to statements which were alluded to yesterday in press reports. However, I can assure the hon. member and the House that we are working toward parity, and this will clearly be one of the matters we shall be discussing not only with United States interests, that is, in terms of government interests, but also with representatives of the automobile industry here in Canada as well, during the meetings now going on in connection with the auto pact.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-POSSIBILITY OF ACHIEVING PRICE PARITY THIS YEAR
speechtext: For the simple reason, Mr. Speaker, that to use those in isolation might put in jeopardy the whole concept of the auto pact. Nevertheless, I want to know from the companies in specific terms why the gap exists, and it is for that reason that I am initiating talks with them.

speechtext:

Oral Questions
licence holders will receive notification that their lobster fishing privileges have been called into question.
In view of the controversy created by this announcement, is it the minister's intention to make a statement on this matter in the House, or will he convene a special meeting of the Fisheries and Forestry Committee in order to explain the yardstick to be used by his officials when determining those who will be permitted to continue lobster fishing in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, both suggestions have merit. There is a committee to hear their appeals. I have said very clearly that this policy will be applied in the most flexible way possible. But there is one basic fact, and that is we are trying to preserve the stocks of lobster for those whose livelihood depends on fishing and not for those who are involved in other professions and other types of industrial work.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT   JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
that the bill be read the third time and do pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, may I address the House briefly at the third reading stage of Bill C-71 and recommend the adoption of this bill on third reading. As hon. members know, the bill went to the committee. It incorporates a number of desirable changes in the Criminal Code, but it will be impossible for me at third reading to discuss all those changes which were examined so carefully by the committee. As hon. members know, the bill was first introduced on July 17 last. During the fall session of parliament, before Christmas, it received careful study in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and was reported back to the House just before Christmas. I am most grateful for the work done by the members of the Justice and legal affairs committee and grateful for the assistance they have given me with this bill.
This afternoon I shall mention only four aspects of Bill C-71, namely, provisions relating to juries and courts of appeal, those relating to amendments to the Bail Reform Act, amendments relating to organized crime and amendments relating to drinking drivers. Once these amendments are proclaimed and become law, it will no longer be possible for a court composed of a judge and jury to have its verdict of acquittal reversed and a conviction substituted by an appellate tribunal. The jury system has throughout the years, and for generations, proven to be a system that produces justice which is both understood and accepted in our society. If hon. members accept what is proposed in this bill, the law will be clear and in future a person who chooses trial by jury can only be convicted by a jury.
While the particular case which brought this issue to a head involved the prosecution of Dr. Morgentaler for a violation of the abortion provisions of the Criminal Code, the fundamental principle involved in the amendment sweeps beyond the controversy that swirls about those provisions of the Criminal Code relating to abortion.
Second, I want to touch on the subject of bail. With respect to the bail reform legislation which was enacted in 1972, the legislation reflects amendments which are considered desirable in the light of experience since 1972. Since becoming Minister of Justice, I find, after talking to
21 130-34

January 27, 1976
Criminal Code
lawyers, including defence lawyers, citizens, judges, prosecutors and police officers, that much concern has been expressed that people who are dangerous to society are obtaining bail too easily. Over and over, in criticizing the criminal justice system, people say to me, "Mr. Basford, we agree with the underlying principle of the Bail Reform Act, but it is being abused and taken advantage of."
The amendments which are incorporated in this legislation are badly needed and have general acceptance and endorsement both at the federal and provincial levels. The law must also seek to protect society as well as the accused, and it seems not unreasonable to me to require that certain types of accused should have to convince the magistrate that they should be released on bail. It seems not unreasonable to me that certain classes of accused persons should have the onus put on them to show that they should be released. Pursuant to the amendments now before the House, those on whom the onus would fall would include, first, those who while out on bail commit another offence under the Criminal Code; second, those who violate the bail provisions upon which they are out; third, non-residents of Canada; fourth, those charged with murder; and fifth, those trafficking in or importing narcotics or conspiring to traffick in or import narcotics. It seems self- evident that society at large is entitled to the assurance that those five groups will not be granted bail without first having to convince a magistrate or judge that they should be granted bail.
The general rule under the Bail Reform Act remains. It is, I think, a good principle. It remains the rule for all other accused persons, that is, for those who have been arrested. If an accused has been arrested, he should be released unless the Crown satisfies the magistrate that detention is necessary to ensure that the accused will appear at his trial, and that it is necessary for the safety or protection of the public: this may include consideration of any substantial likehood that he will commit a second criminal offence. That is to say, all classes of accused other than the ones mentioned will be released under the provisions of the Bail Reform Act of 1972 unless the Crown can show that there is a likehood thct they will not appear for trial after they have been released, and that detention is necessary in the interests of the protection and safety of the public, which includes the likelihood that they will commit a second offence and therefore should not be released.
My concern in moving the amendments in Bill C-71 and the further amendments I moved in committee was to ensure the protection of the public against the likelihood that the accused would commit another offence while out on bail. As hon. members know, however, we in this House can write all the laws we want, but if they are not argued by police or by Crown counsel and are not properly applied by magistrates, they will not effectively protect the public interest in accordance with the principles that underlie the legislation. These amendments, when proclaimed, will give to police officers and to prosecutors a proper legislative basis upon which to argue the granting of bail. Obviously, if they cannot meet that test provided in the legislation, the accused should be out on bail.
Any tightening of the bail provisions may mean that more accused are in custody awaiting trial, although the

objective of these new provisions is to protect the public from such persons while awaiting their trial. It is essential, in the interest of justice, that everything possible be done to speed up the process between the time of arrest and trial, and not only to speed up that process, in the interest of those who are ultimately found to be innocent, but also to avoid some of the game-playing that goes on in court by professional criminals and their advisers. Of course, the more delay between the time of arrest and the time of either declaration of innocence or conviction, adds to the immense cost to the taxpayer and to the cost of the whole administration of the criminal justice system. Therefore, it is essential that at the federal level, parliament, and the local levels, positive steps be taken to ensure that the process between arrest and acquittal or conviction is as effective and speedy as possible. Bill C-71 contains some provisions that will assist in that regard.
The measures relating to summary conviction trial, the elimination of grand juries in all provinces except Nova Scotia, the provisions relating to absconding offenders during preliminary hearing or trial, the changing of the eight-day rule on adjournment, and the provisions relating to loss of jurisdiction are some measures that are no longer required for the protection of the accused before the courts.
Obviously, this is only an initial step in the much larger process of reducing the time between arrest and trial and of improving the whole process of the criminal justice system. I am looking at steps within my department, in terms of reorganization, by which it can be more effective toward this end. I am discussing, examining and exploring with members of the federal Law Reform Commission what they can do in terms of recommendations to speed up the process between arrest and trial. At the moment, I am quietly talking with provincial attorneys general because, of course, much of the question of administration of justice is clearly within their jurisdiction. We are discussing ways in which we can work together to accomplish this end. I have pointed out the provisions in Bill C-71 which I think are important with regard to changes to the Bail Reform Act to overcome what I view as very legitimate criticisms of the original legislation which has been open to abuse and taken advantage of.
I want to address myself briefly to the question of organized crime. As hon. members know, the activities of organized crime in some parts of this country have come very dramatically to light and public attention by reason of the provincial commission of inquiry into organized crime in the province of Quebec. One of the problems in this connection is the ease with which the procedures of crime, including organized crime, may be hidden and diverted from the law enforcement process through laundering devices.
Hon. members will appreciate that in the area of commercial fraud, more and more sophistication is being brought to bear. With a view to counter-attacking in that field, Bill C-71 provides an amendment by which it will be possible to deal with what is generally known as laundering of moneys acquired by unlawful conduct. The essence of the proposed amendment strikes at criminal activity on a national and international scale. Under current law, it is an offence to be in possession of property obtained illegal-
January 27, 1976

ly whether in Canada or elsewhere. Under the proposed amendment, it will also be an offence to be in possession of proceeds of any property obtained by an offence committed either in Canada or elsewhere. For example, stocks and bonds might be converted into forms of property and passed through various companies which appear to be legitimate but are actually controlled by organized crime, thus hiding from detection. The amendment would allow those proceeds, or fruits of organized crime to fall within the ambit of the Criminal Code and the ambit of our law enforcement officers.
The amendment relating to organized crime is, as hon. members know, under these provisions. The growing international nature of criminal activity has prompted a new provision of the Criminal Code whereby it is made an offence to conspire in Canada to commit an offence out of Canada, and to make it an offence to conspire out of Canada to commit an offence in Canada. Regarding the first case, Canada should take a stand against those who use Canada as a planning base for criminal activities. An example of the first situation would be where directors of a company incorporated in Canada conspire in Canada to fleece members of the public or investors in another country, bringing great disrepute upon legitimate Canadian investment dealers and investment promotion.
The second case is aimed at deterring people who may or may not be Canadian citizens and who plan criminal activities in another country for actual execution in Canada. An example of the second case is where persons abroad conspire to commit in Canada acts of violence whether or not such acts are criminal in the country where the conspiracy takes place. For example, a group of terrorists could conspire outside Canada to commit acts of terrorism within Canada.
In relation to organized crime, I mention just in passing the measures relating to the obliteration of serial numbers which assist law enforcement officers in relation to some international aspects of car thieves, and measures relating to making this an offence. I am paraphrasing the legislation. This bill makes it an offence knowingly to use stolen or fraudulently obtained credit cards which, again, are a device of national and international crime.
The fourth point I want to raise with regard to Bill C-71 relates to drinking and driving. As hon. members are aware, parliament in 1969 adopted the breathalyzer test and made it an offence for a person to have in his system .08 per cent of alcohol while driving. The legislation also provided that where a peace officer had reasonable grounds to believe that someone was impaired, he could require him to submit to a breathalyzer test. If the person refused, the refusal in itself constituted an offence. The new amendments are designed to enable law enforcement authorities more readily to identify persons who because of their alcoholic condition should not be on the road.
It should be borne in mind that roadside screening does not in itself establish guilt or innocence, but is merely an aid to indicate whether or not a driver should be required to submit himself to a breathalyzer test. The roadside screening test can only be applied when a peace officer has reasonable cause to suspect that the driver has alcohol in
Criminal Code
his body. I believe that the awful carnage precipitated by drinking and driving on our streets and highways, partly because of drinking drivers, is in itself justification for what these amendments propose. One need only be reminded of the facts to recognize the seriousness of the situation. In 1974, 6,000 deaths occurred on our highways, and 230,000 injuries. The amount of $1.3 billion was lost because of these deaths, $1 billion were lost as a result of absence from work associated with traffic accidents, and medical bills amounted to $250 million.
It is often impossible to say how many of these deaths and injuries are directly related to drinking drivers, but we do know that the proportion is high. It seems to me, therefore, that this alarming and awful carnage which is reflected almost daily in headlines in our newspapers is in itself justification for what these amendments propose as a means of providing law enforcement agencies across the country with a proper and legal basis to run roadside screening tests to deter those who drive an automobile after having taken alcohol.
I am sure hon. members will recognize the areas I have touched upon today as areas of serious concern to law-abiding citizens everywhere. The bill before us contains a number of other amendments which have been discussed both in this House and in committee. I emphasize that all the amendments are designed to improve the present law in one way or another. Some are purely technical in nature. Others-and these are the ones which I trust will be particularly welcomed by professionals and laymen alike- will contribute to the protection and control of individual as well as organized criminals.
In closing, I wish to thank the members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for their work in carefully examining this bill in committee. I commend the measure to the House and hope it will pass in an orderly way so that its provisions may be proclaimed and this country may have the advantage of the improvements it contains.

speechtext:
I am very happy that the new Minister of Justice has sufficient flexibility of mind to enable him to accept the suggestion made by the right hon. member for Prince Albert and, of course, by other members of the House who joined with him. Once again, I congratulate the Minister of Justice. I hope that in exercising the kind of discretion he exercised the other day, he will bear in mind
2 1 1 30-3414

January 27, 1976
Criminal Code
another matter which is before him now, the Latta case, concerning a member of my own profession, a distinguished scholar, a professor at Queen's University who was convicted in the city of Edmonton by judge and jury of the very serious charge of murder.
I wish to refer to this matter for a few moments before we consider some of the changes in the Criminal Code, because it is relevant to what I have in mind. One of the greatest problems related to appeals in serious criminal cases is that unless there has been a mistake in law by the judge in instructing a jury, or unless-this is very rare- the decision of the jury is so perverse that this in itself becomes a question of law, it is seldom if ever that a court of appeal will upset a verdict.
I mention this having regard to the seriousness of the case and many submissions which are now being made, in the hope that the Minister of Justice, having made use of an unusual procedure in granting Mr. Morgentaler a new trial, will not be deterred from exercising the same kind of ministerial discretion on other occasions when the need arises. It may be that he will be subject to some criticism. It may be suggested that if he were to do the same thing twice in one year, or twice during his tenure of office, he would be following a new kind of practice. But I maintain that these are unique cases, cases which call for the kind of assessment which has been made by the Minister of Justice.
I wish now, on third reading of this bill, to put forward a few facts in relation to the increase in crime. I hope that the Minister of Justice, who inherited this legislation from the former minister of justice-hon. members will recall that when he first took on the job he talked about bringing laws before parliament to control the ever-increasing crime rate-did not leave the impression, and I am sure he would not do so, with the public at large that Bill C-71 is the instrument he had in mind to bring about these necessary amendments to the law to stamp out organized crime and reverse the present tendency of the crime rate to increase.
I want to put a few facts on the record having to do with the increase in crime, and I wish the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) were here while I do so. In 1974-75 the murder rate in Canada went up by 18.8 per cent. Breaking and entering increased from 48,625 in 1974 to 54,982 in 1975, that is, a rise of 11.3 per cent-something like inflation. Consider the increase which has taken place in the crime of robbery with violence. We have heard a lot of talk about legislation to control the possession of handguns and other firearms. It is like Alice in Wonderland: jam yesterday, jam tomorrow, but never jam today. The present Minister of Justice can be distinguished from the former minister and the one before that. He is one Minister of Justice who did practice law. He has had some experience at the bar as defence counsel. I do not know whether he ever prosecuted or not, but he is one Minister of Justice who isn't all theory.
In 1974 there were 1,214 robberies with violence and firearms, and in 1975, 2,106. That is an increase in crimes of robbery with firearms and guns of 70.9 per cent in one year. Crime is on the increase.

Kidnapping is one of the worst types of crime society is facing today. People who are in responsible positions and getting a salary like the former minister of finance, of $200,000 a year, are always in danger of their children being kidnapped when they leave school or go to the park, or their wives being kidnapped for purposes of extortion. Not long ago I raised the case in the House of a girl who was kidnapped, put into the trunk of a car and kept there for nine or ten hours while the car was put in the garage. She was very lucky to survive. Across the line a very important case concerning Patty Hearst is commencing with the picking of the jury. Kidnapping and extortion are the worst type of crime; they are a plague and a blight on people who cannot defend themselves. Kidnappings increased in 1974 by 40.1 per cent, so I hope something will be done to provide in our law a deterrent to this crime. Before leaving that subject, every person in public life is in danger of having members of his family kidnapped, and so are others who are not able to defend themselves as we may be able to. With regard to rape convictions, there were 348 in 1974, an increase of only 4.3 per cent. Crimes of rape, kidnapping, robbery with firearms, breaking and entering and homicide are all on the increase.
My good friend the Minister of Justice dealt with bail reform, which he would be the first to admit the former minister of justice introduced. I think all practising lawyers realize that bail should be the right of every citizen, but it is a right that has to be used with some caution. As the minister said today, there are many cases in big cities of a person out on bail committing the same kind of crime with which he had been charged, perhaps in a different place and under different circumstances, and he does so several times before the first offense is brought to trial. I am glad that that hole in the bucket has been plugged.
I want to bring to the attention of the House something that happened over the Christmas recess. I was telephoned by some newspaper people in connection with a case in the city of Hamilton. It had to do with the law we passed regarding wiretapping. I had some reservations about putting so many "ifs" and "buts" into that law. Although it is very easy to criticize it, it is far easier to see the weaknesses of a law once it is in operation.
I understand that certain police officers obtained authorization through the Crown attorney, under the act, to obtain an order to wiretap a telephone conversation. I believe that the chief or the deputy chief of the city-I do not know his name, since I was called on the telephone- discovered that one of his chief officers was involved in syndicated crime. When the Crown attorney attempted to put in the record of the telephone conversation as evidence, the defence, and properly so-I will not bother to read the section of the Code-objected to it on the ground that they had not obtained authorization regarding the other party to the conversation who was talking to the police officer, and so the evidence was ruled inadmissible.
As a result, a very responsible and highly placed public official, one who administers the law of this country in that city, had the telephone conversation been put in as evidence would have been connected with some syndicated crime, yet he walks the streets today an innocent man. I have had similar experiences, as I know have the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), the hon. member
January 27, 1976

for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) and other lawyers, where you can successfully defend a man on some technical ground of this nature. The law must be administered fairly and squarely.
My point is this, Mr. Speaker. All of us are for reform. We all want to see the best system of justice. None of us wants to read about the sort of thing raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn)-solitary confinement in jails and poor conditions in our penitentiaries. We want to better those conditions. But at the same time, particularly at this period in our society, we must weigh very carefully the reforms we do bring in. Such reforms might have been beneficial a few years ago, but today, with the new kind of criminal mind and syndicated crime, we must not allow some pretty dangerous people to go free so that they can plague society with the kind of behaviour to which all of us who are trying to be law-abiding citizens object.
When the minister took office he said-I do not think I am misquoting him-that he would bring in laws, which he would ask parliament to pass, that would control crime. I have already indicated the percentage growth of crime in one year. I realize the minister inherited this bill, but I hope he has other measures in mind for controlling crime, particularly kidnapping which is on the increase, and extortion which is a horrible crime.
I should like to refer to one thing the minister said when he was before the committee. I think he was advised by the president of the Canadian Bar Association so he would not be saying anything that was incorrect. Several members of the Canadian Bar criminal law section gave evidence before the committee and I want to put on record what the president said about the Canadian Bar. Although I think we should always get direction from the Canadian Bar and the Bar Associations, and without being at all critical in saying this, often the presidents of those associations have a civil law or corporate law practice and are not experienced in the rules of evidence and the terms and provisions of the Criminal Code.
I think the impression was left that the president of the Canadian Bar Association endorsed the changes that were made, but the head of the criminal section of that association had this to say at page 26 of committee report No. 32 for December 4, 1975:
There was some comment in one of the issues of a house journal of the Canadian Bar Association which indicated to me as a reader, and I believe to my colleagues, that the president of the Canadian Bar Association was basically in favour of Bill C-71. The then president was Mr. Somerville. Certainly it is our position that he did not speak for us. We were not consulted. We do not think that he consulted the criminal justice subsection of the Canadian Bar Association, particularly in view of the resolutions which were later published in the same organ but in a later issue. We feel that there is no excuse or no reason to believe that the practising members of the bar, the criminal bar, who belong to the Canadian Bar Association feel any differently than we do about these amendments.
He criticizes some amendments that I will deal with right now. What I wanted to point out was that the criminal section of the Canadian Bar Association did not endorse some of the changes that have been made. What are some of the changes that have been made? I have dealt
Criminal Code
previously with some of these, so I can do so now quite briefly.
I endorse the change in reference to corroboration under the rape section. I would go even further than that in respect of the right of defence counsel to cross examine the complainant regarding her past sexual experience with others or the person named in the complaint. As the new amendment is worded, the judge can grant leave if he finds it is material to the defence of the accused. I think that is good, but I would issue this caution, a caution I have often repeated: rape is one of the easiest charges to lay and it is sometimes one of the most difficult to defend. The whole thing hinges basically on the question of consent. I have pointed out very carefully during any discussions about this subject that even a prostitute can be raped. This involves basically the question of consent.
The removal of the right to cross examination is good, because often the complainant is treated more like the accused and it is very difficult for a female to give evidence under those circumstances. On the other hand, I hope the courts will consider very carefully these exceptions. There may be cases where this is necessary, because a conviction under the rape section is a very serious thing and carries a penalty of life imprisonment, depending on the circumstances. In endorsing that amendment, that is a caution I would put forward.
Let me go into something else for a moment. This has reference to the breathalyzer test. There is not a member of parliament nor a member of the legislature, whatever his political views may be, who would not agree with the Minister of Justice and many other speakers who have said that alcohol and gasoline just do not mix, or that the incidence of accidents in the cities, particularly those with heavy traffic, increases proportionately to the amount of alcohol consumed.
On the other hand, one has to exercise a little caution when changing the law in respect of liquor. I guess I am being pretty brave with my political life when I say this because I may receive some criticism as all the publicity has been in favour of the use of the breathalyzer. But we must remember that it is certainly against our common law when we change the concept of a person being innocent until being proven guilty. The breathalyzer is a good thing, but once you have been forced to take a breathalyzer test you have to go on the stand in your own defence. You may be totally innocent but belong to the Civil Rights Committee of Canada and refuse to take a breathalyzer test, and in that event you are guilty. The first offence may involve a fine, but on a second conviction you will go to jail, and on a third conviction you are liable to imprisonment for three months.
Like many others, I have asked the Minister of Justice why he has included this mandatory sentence. I asked the Minister of Justice, in respect of violence with the use of firearms, why he did not also include a mandatory jail term of a number of years in the penitentiary. Surely there should be some such penalty for extortion and kidnapping. The minister has said that he has never believed in a system with that kind of jurisprudence, even in criminal cases, because he has felt this should be left to the discretion of the criminal judge in sentencing. Let me go very quickly to the point I am trying to make. Surely if we are

January 27, 1976
Criminal Code
to have a mandatory sentence in respect of a second conviction for refusing to take a breathalyzer test, we should have a mandatory prison sentence for people convicted of going into banks and kidnapping children and wives for the purpose of extortion. That seems only logical.
Let me say something about the sale and consumption of liquor in this country. I suppose it is true to say that many of us have been called to many bars. Let me point out the hypocrisy of many governments, and I am not referring particularly to this government. In 1974 the federal government took in, through excise duty and customs tariffs on liquor, $278,140,199.83. In 1975 the people were much more dry and much more thirsty, and the federal government obtained revenue from the sale of liquor amounting to $310,915,395, an increase of about 11.8 per cent. I do not have similar figures in respect of provincial revenues, but I have read articles that would indicate the provinces take in about the same amount.
One only has to go to the embassies in this country to find out how much tax is being charged on a bottle of liquor. I understand the embassies pay $2 or $2.25 for a bottle of liquor for which I pay $7.85 at the liquor store- when I go, which is not that often.

speechtext:
Someone points out that that is pretty cheap stuff. The point I want to make is that governments are getting millions of dollars a year from the sale and consumption of alcohol in one form or another. The provinces have jurisdiction over various cocktail lounges and all sorts of outlets. All the provinces and the federal government have to do is sit back and wait for the revenue to roll in.
All the police in this country have to do is sit and wait for people to come out of these bars or to leave their country clubs after playing golf some afternoon. I do not know where we would find all the jails to hold all these people if every one of them was given a breathalyzer test. One only has to drink two average drinks of two ounces or one and a half ounces to come within the limit. What I am suggesting is that there is a great deal of hypocrisy on the part of governments of this country, because the more the people drink the more revenue governments obtain, yet the same governments have almost adopted a policy of prohibition in respect of drinking offences. There has to be some balance.
The thing I do not like about this new section is that it says the peace officer must have a reasonable suspicion before requiring an individual to take a breathalyzer test. In the criminal law as it stood, the peace officer had to have reasonable and probable grounds for such belief. An officer could not just stop anyone that he felt should take a breathalyzer test. The hypocrisy lies in the fact that the peace officer must now only have a reasonable suspicion. So road blocks can be set up and there is no difficulty. If one does not take a breathalyzer test, one pays a fine on the first occasion and on the second and third occasions one goes to jail for a period of up to two years. I think that is correct; yes, it is imprisonment for not more than two years.

If it is right to lay down those penalties, then it is right to have mandatory, minimum penalties for people who commit rape, armed robbery with violence, or use firearms. We cannot have it only one way. A great deal of advertising and promotion has been going on day after day and week after week on television. I know severe steps must be taken to stop the mixture of gasoline and of alcohol, and we are dealing with that. However, when we deal with the law, the law must be practical and, above all, it must be just. It can be just only if it is just in respect of all offences. Why should we pick out merely that one? There is not even a minimum sentence, under certain circumstances, for criminal negligence of manslaughter. Those are the things which concern me.
There is one other point I should like to make. The new law is quite flexible. Appeals from summary convictions are called trials de novo. A trial by summary conviction means that the person is charged with a lesser offence. The Crown may charge a person with an indictable offence, which involves a more severe penalty than summary conviction. If a person is convicted on summary conviction, the appeal is from the provincial judge, formerly the magistrate, to the district court, and all the evidence may be presented again. The whole matter is reviewed in the form of a brand new trial. In fact, witnesses may be called, at the appeal to the district court, who had not been called previously.
I suppose there has been some abuse of that practice, because lawyers sometimes would have a trial run before a provincial judge and then go to the district court. There is something I wish to point out which I know the minister and hon. members who have practised law understand. In the provincial courts, judges have to sit all morning. Anyone who attends these courts will realize how many cases a judge hears in a day. The judge does not have time to weigh all the pros and cons. There is, of course, the safeguard that in exceptional cases the whole thing can be reviewed by the district court. In some cases the magistrate merely says, on the basis that the Crown witnesses and policemen are honest, that he finds the accused guilty. That is a finding of fact and there is no appeal unless there is a rehearing and a re-evaluation of the witnesses.
That is the weakness of our system. A judge who is a friend of mine, in many cases takes the position that wherever the plaintiff's evidence differs from that of the defendant, he accepts the evidence of the plaintiff. Then the court of appeal is in the position of having to say it is sorry, but the judge has clearly decided the facts and the appeal is on those facts. The court of appeal points out that the judge did not believe the evidence on one side but he believed the evidence on the other side. We got this half a loaf from the minister. We are all happy that he repented. He said the law would be left similar to what it is, but that there will be an application to a district court to direct whether or not there shall be a new trial.
There is only one flaw in that. Knowing judges as I do- many of them are good friends of mine and I hope they remain so-they are liable to say that they do not want all the hard work involved, and very often will not exercise the discretion. It will become a very rare discretion, if ever it is used. I am not at all happy with that amendment, but
January 27, 1976

it is better than no loaf. We can only hope that the rules in respect of that kind of discretion will be made by judicial law.
Having said that, our party accepts the changes in the Code. I have pointed out some weaknesses. Some of the weaknesses I have pointed out are my own ideas. On the whole it is good legislation. My last word to the minister is that if he has a package with which he thinks he can cut out or reduce crime, I wish he would bring it forward, because he inherited this from the former minister and he must have a package somewhere which he can bring in. He said he would bring in legislation to look after crime. I would hope, when he is thinking about that, we might have the same kind of royal commission or inquiry they have had in the province of Quebec to find out where all the crime lies. Had we not had that inquiry in the province of Quebec we would never have known about all the bad meat. Why, in the name of justice, the Liberal federal government challenged the legislation, the authority and the jurisdiction is beyond my comprehension, because that opened a can of worms. I am glad they held the inquiry. We have been begging for the same thing on a federal basis.
I am glad to see the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) here, because he has a good point. The other evening I watched a psychiatrist on television who said that the human mind at a certain age is exposed to violence day after day and hour after hour. He said this will affect the mind and some people will resort to violence. I understand that Miss Judy LaMarsh is conducting a very important inquiry in the province of Ontario. I hope the federal government will follow suit and have a similar inquiry across the nation to find out what effect this has on the children. This psychiatrist went further than I would. Had I said that, I would have been accused of being a redneck or something similar. The psychiatrist said that the exposure of youth in the drug stores to pornography hour after hour and week after week may be the reason that the number of rape cases is so high. He went that far. I do not know if that is right, but I do say we should set up an inquiry to find out what some of the experts in these fields feel about this problem. Maybe if we had those facts, the people who draft the legislation under the direction of the minister would be able to bring in some laws to clean up society.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT   JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, first of all, to congratulate the minister on a very sensitive, compassionate and sensible judicial decision in the Morgentaler case. I want to start off by giving the minister a pat on the back so that he will be in a better position in respect of some of the other remarks I shall make.
I think we should speak for a while in the House about the things that are not contained in the bill. I know the answer the minister will give is that we should wait. As the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) said, it is jam tomorrow. The minister will say that this omnibus bill will solve all our problems. I have been here since 1972, and I and all members are waiting to see what kind of approach the government will take to crime. We must talk in this House from time to time about the causes of crime. After listening to the hon. member for Calgary North, I must say I am sometimes confused in respect of some of his
Criminal Code
comments about crime, but I want to give him credit for what I believe to be a very progressive statement he made on second reading of this bill. We may disagree from time to time about the right approach in terms of penalties, but I think the causes of crime he outlined in Hansard on November 18 should be repeated in this House because I think he covered one of the real problems which we are not attacking. This is what he said:
-I have felt for years that we must get at the breeding grounds of crime. What are those breeding grounds? Crime breeds in cesspools of injustice. Wherever there is injustice, crime will breed. It breeds in the urban slums or in the fast-growing cities of Canada. Urban poverty makes people the victims, not the masters, of their environment. A bad environment becomes the hereditary property of succeeding generations. When I travel to various areas of this city, I see children who are forced to play on concrete and cement without necessary parks which are large enough to be playgrounds. The situation is worse here than it is in Calgary. These children are brought up in conditions which foster crime.
That is a very progressive statement on the subject of crime. If we are to deal with the causes, we must not only examine where criminals come from but we must examine who they are. I would suggest that if anyone goes to our maximum security institutions where we find the worst offenders, those people about whom we cannot do anything, it will be found that the average prisoner there has an education of about grade 6. These people have been rejected, first by their families, then by their school and then by their peers. So they isolate themselves into a tiny group. That group is consistently made up of people with a strong ego and high intelligence, people who are anti-social and quite often with a learning disability. Also, quite often they are mentally ill. One could ask how they became mentally ill, whether our institutions have made them that way or whether they were that way before.
What I do not see in the bill, and what I am hoping the minister will attend to perhaps in the next bill, are the M'Naghten rules. I hope he will take another look at the question of whether we are applying a proper standard in terms of those who are mentally ill and are committing crimes, because I can tell you that in the maximum security institution in my riding a great many of those people should be in maximum security in a mental hospital and not in a penal institution which is not able to provide any help for them. I am not suggesting they should be released; I am suggesting that many of those who have damaged psyches should be under treatment and should not be placed in solitary confinement, and they should not be released until we are satisfied that they have recovered.
There are people in those institutions with paranoid delusions about the people who put them there, about the defence and prosecuting lawyers and about the judges. They are ill and they can be dangerous if released. What I am saying is that we should take another look at the M'Naghten rules. We should get back to the question of whether anti-social behaviour is the result of mental aberration and whether it should be treated, or considered a crime and punished. I look forward to a reassessment of that question.
I am disappointed at the fact that when the minister came to the question of organized crime, he did not mention the co-ordinated law enforcement unit in British

January 27, 1976
Criminal Code
Columbia which I think should be given some credit. John Hogarth and his group in British Columbia have really done an excellent job, and I am pleased to see that the new government in B.C. is carrying on the program of co-operation at all levels to get to the top of the drug rings and to move up in the scale of people we arrest, because up to now we continue simply to catch the small fry, which does not really solve any of these criminal problems.
One of the things that is not in the bill, and it concerns me a great deal-I know it concerned the hon. member for Calgary North on second reading-is the question of publicity during a trial and the effect that such publicity can have on an individual. When I was defending people while practicing law, I knew that the fact that the name of the man who was charged appeared in the newspaper was as good as a conviction, because the penalty for a person who is brought into total disgrace in his community through being charged with an offence and having his name published can often be worse than the conviction itself.
We had this tragedy in Ottawa not too long ago when a person charged with a sexual offence committed suicide because of the nature of the alleged offence and the terrific embarrassment to him and his family. We in the profession often are so closed in in our own little world and are so closed in in the game of the adversary system in the courts that we sometimes forget the human realities of the people whom we represent and we forget the effect on them.
I say that that is a violation of the presumption of innocence to a very serious extent because, although I do not disagree with the public's right to know, what I say is that the public's right to know is not necessarily the instant that the charge is laid. So long as the information reaches the public, the principle of freedom of speech and the principle of the open court system is not eroded.
I am pleased to see the minister paying such close attention to the debate, and I hope he will take another look at the matter of the right of the public to be informed and when it should be informed. The refusal to publish the proceedings of preliminary hearings can be very useful both from the point of view of the defence and the prosecution. When you are defending someone who is charged with an offence-let us assume that he is charged with a sallacious offence such as indecent assault on a young person-surely letting the public know who this person in their midst is after conviction is soon enough. Doing so beforehand is tantamount to sentencing that person to purgatory for the rest of his life. Sometimes the press is most insensitive in its anxiety to see that all the information is released. People from the press are sometimes terribly insensitive regarding the right of the individual to some privacy in a serious situation.
Another area that we should consider, in terms of publicity, is the effect not merely on juries but on the whole public of violent and sallacious reporting such as we get in some of our worst magazines. I am not referring to the major dailies, which tend to be a little more responsible, but I look with sadness at some of the publications we see on our local newsstands which use crime in a most exploitive way and which pander to the worst emotions in the population. That could clearly affect the judgment of a jury picked for a trial in such a case. So I am asking that the minister give serious consideration to redesigning the
[Mr. Leggatt.)
rules concerning publicity around the courts, particularly with regard to charges that are laid.
I want to say a word or two about the individual in our society who, either through brain damage or bad environment-no matter how it happened-is incapable of feeling any remorse for his crime or compassion for the victims of his crime. It seems to me that if we are going to make any progress in terms of reducing the incidence of horror and crime in this country, we will have to identify the psychotic, dangerous personality much earlier. That does not mean to suggest that punitive action should be taken earlier. It simply means that an assessment should be made such as we do for those with learning disabilities and other problems in schools. Let us try to identify someone who is acting in an anti-social way in the early days of his school life, and see whether some assistance can be brought to the community to prevent the kind of dangerous and violent activity which occurs. Admittedly, there are very few such people, but there are enough to make our society feel suspicious that we are under attack by criminals.
The right answer for those who are worried about a break-in of their house, or a mugging, is not to get a dog, lock the door and buy a gun; the right answer is total community response to the problem of crime, the community working co-operatively toward a solution. I have talked in this House many times about the proliferation of guns and the fact that it is not a solution to crime. Not only does it not solve crime, but it does not provide any protection to the individual. Anyone coming to your house to break in will probably bring a gun along for protection if he thinks you have one. In fact, at the moment the chances of being robbed are greater if it is known that you have a gun, because that is one of the things most people in the business of breaking and entering are seeking.
I am concerned about some of the things that are not in this bill, Mr. Speaker. The law reform commission's study on local enforcement in the Toronto area should be looked at. Statistics on declining crime in that project area showed that through community involvement, instead of throwing everybody into jail or charging them, the number of family disputes and minor crimes has dropped. Our police must be part of the community and not be isolated in cars. I should like to see the policeman back on the beat, knowing everybody in his community so that a rapport or relationship could develop and he could prevent crime before it occured.
Our emphasis continues to be on increasing penalties after the crime occurs. We should move into the area of prevention through the local police officer anticipating the problems in his area. He can only do that if he knows the people and develops a personal, friendly relationship with those for whom he is responsible. There is no point in giving the policeman the responsibility for enforcement of traffic regulations in the whole city of Vancouver when he should be maintaining law and order and preventing crime in an area known to him and where he is known to the people who live there.
I should like to say a word or two about the bill itself, Mr. Speaker. This party supports it. We think some of the provisions are progessive and some of the drafting of the
January 27, 1976

bail reform provisions is excellent. One provision on which I have not heard too much comment is begging while armed. This has been a major problem in the Vancouver area, I do not know about other areas, and the minister is to be congratulated for responding to the problem.
I have some reservations about the changes in the impaired driving provisions. In a sense, mandatory penalties are an erosion of judicial discretion. Perhaps those judges who have complained from time to time about the mandatory sentencing provisions should look at the way they co-ordinate sentences. Our of the reasons for mandatory sentencing in Canada is that the public is obviously dissatisfied with the penalties imposed by the courts. If we could better co-ordinate sentences and the reasons for sentencing, perhaps we would not need a mandatory sentencing provision. Quite often in a case where there is real merit, where a mandatory sentence should not be imposed, the courts have no discretion and as a result there is severe injustice.
I am not upset about the increase in mandatory penalties in view of the epidemic of driving offences in the country. I think a lot of people have reservations about the roadside screening provision, however. That is clearly a departure from the normal responsibility of the police officer to have both reasonable and probable grounds to conduct an investigation. I sympathize with the minister on this. It is a massive problem in Canada and I believe we will need more roadside screening in order to reduce the present carnage on the highways. I should like to see the minister use his influence with cabinet to apply to accident prevention the huge liquor profits and taxes that accrue to both the federal and provincial governments.
I should like to say something else about liquor, Mr. Speaker. In cases of motor manslaughter, where the driver had too much to drink, it is sometimes difficult to get a conviction. Some members of the jury may be saying, "There, but for the grace of God, go I". There is considerable sympathy for the accused. Sometimes members of the public get upset about acquittals in cases of criminal negligence. They do not understand that in this country we are all guilty of drinking liquor. It is a problem to judge how much liquor one can drink and then whether one should drive.

speechtext:
Especially at $7.80 a quart as the hon. member for Calgary North suggested. But, Mr. Speaker, because it is such a culturally acceptable activity it is difficult for the Crown to get a conviction in a liquor offence. If you have 12 drinkers on a jury, you have a job on your hands. I think we should take note of the fact that we are heavy drinkers in this country. The hon. member for Calgary North suggested that in his area the country clubs were being screened and that police waited outside to catch people going home after a pleasant evening. That has been going on in the beer parlours in my riding for a long time. The police have been pretty thorough in picking up drinkers, but I am a little tired of beer parlour operators
Criminal Code
allowing people to stagger out of their premises and into a car, to be immediately picked up.
Surely there is some responsibility on the part of those who sell liquor to be careful about how much people have had to drink. Surely they should cut them off before it is too late. There have been instances where people have been helped out of a hotel, got into a car and then were arrested when they left the parking lot. I think those who operate hotels had better accept more responsibility in terms of preventing carnage on the highways.
I am delighted with the provision on theft under $200 which will now become a summary conviction offence. This is long overdue. People involved in shoplifting or offences of a minor nature formerly had a record of an indictable offence and this affected their future when applying for a job with a major corporation or the civil service. Shoplifting has been a widespread epidemic and the discretion to make it a summary conviction offence is useful. Actually, in some circumstances kleptomaniacs who may have engaged in stealing could be granted a conditional discharge where appropriate.

speechtext: Where is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) (Rosedale))? The hon. member has exactly described the fiscal policies of the government.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT   JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
In this country it is unlikely that you can obtain much that is worth while for $200 or less. The increased penalty in the cruelty to animals provisions is also worth while, although I do not know why there is a maximum sentence of two years. Cases involving great cruelty to animals could warrant a more severe penalty. I congratulate the government for introducing discretionary powers for taking an animal from its owner because he has been cruel. This provision is particularly useful in cases involving people without the resources to look after animals.
I shall now talk about the rape provisions of the bill. From a legal point of view, these changes are substantial and useful. So far, the Criminal Code has been male oriented and our approach to rape has also been male oriented. I can give hon. members examples of what I mean. I remember a case involving two young lads who were charged with rape. I defended them. They had picked up a girl hitchhiker. I have no sympathy at all for any judge who says to a girl like that, "Why were you hitchhiking?" In that case I think she had a perfect right to hitchhike. Males hitchhike. Why should she be placed in a special category? Why should she be different, merely because she is a female, and not be on the highways? Why should she not be there? The implication of the judge's comment was that she was out there looking for trouble. In that case my clients were acquitted, but for other reasons.

speechtext:
The law was wrong, and I congratulate the minister for recognizing that the law was wrong. At the same time, everyone in this country is presumed innocent until proven guilty, and those engaged in defence work must do their best for their clients. The resources of the Crown are immense. It has the police, all the facilities of the law and all the resources of the state. The defendant has just his lawyer to look after him. We should not say to defence lawyers, "You should not use all the tools available to you." I merely say that the minister has introduced a useful change in the law. Frankly, there is no reason why a female's sexual history should be raised in court. I wonder if the bill goes far enough in changing the rape laws. I suppose we shall have to wait and see.
I now turn to the bail provisions. I think the draftsmanship is excellent. The amendment does not offend anyone's sense of civil liberties and does not negate the principle of presumption of innocence. The onus provision is just about right for dealing with the kinds of problems we face with regard to bail. I have some reservations about the summary conviction appeal provisions, and the abandonment of the trial de novo can make appeals more complicated. The profession was concerned in the past because many people lost their appeals on technicalities. We are still concerned about technicalities and want to see the rights of the accused protected.
When I began my remarks I congratulated the minister for his sensitive and good legal approach to the Morgental-er case, which involves the erosion of the power of juries, and erosion resulting directly from the decision of the Quebec Court of Appeal in that case. I still prefer the judgment of 12 people to the judgment of one man. I particularly trust the judgment of 12 people on questions of fact. Their judgment is based on common, everyday experience. They live the same kind of life as their peer group or the accused may live. I trust people who drink in a beer parlour to find out what happened in a beer parlour.
It was a sad day for the majority of Canadians when the time-honoured system of the jury was eroded by the appellate court decision. Certainly it was a sad day for the majority in the legal profession. Bear in mind that those 
who serve on juries serve at great sacrifice to themselves. They find the work difficult and taxing. If we allow courts of appeal to impose their verdicts on the verdicts of juries, the morale of all jurors will be destroyed. Why take a couple of weeks trying a murder trial, if the court of appeal will not think you smart enough to determine the facts of the case and impose its judgment on the judgment of the jury? I congratulate the minister for adopting exactly the wording of my private member's bill with respect to appeals. I am glad to see the stature of juries restored. However, although there is much good in the bill, there are also weaknesses in it.
I support the call of the hon. member for Calgary North for a commission to look into violence and pornography in society. I am not sure whether the hon. member outlined or suggested terms of reference for the commission. We must recognize that the medium is the message and is massaging the people, as McLuhan said. For example, consider how remarkably similar were the killings that took place at Brampton and the killings that took place in Ottawa recently.
Many crimes of violence depicted on television are duplicated in the community by some poor, sick soul who was inspired by what he saw to do some vicious, antisocial, criminal act. We should also study the effects of pornography. The rape rate is down this year, so that I am not sure if the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary North hold true. But we should study the effects of pornography and see if it dulls the senses. We should not wait for the Ontario commission to report, as there are many other urban areas in Canada. I urge the minister to give serious consideration to setting up a proper inquiry into the effects of violence as depicted on television, on radio and in the newspapers, and the effects of pornography as depicted by those three media. Particularly, let us look at the movie industry which is depicting hard-core pornography and has been for some time.
We must again look at the people in our institutions and ask ourselves what effect our laws will have on them and why they were sent there in the first place. The public's first reaction to violent crime is either to urge that the criminal be hanged, or that we lock him up and throw away the key. We should not ignore these options, because they are valid options at which we should look, but we must think about prevention. These are not preventive measures at all. We must get back to the question of the kind of society we live in. We live in a highly competitive society, a dog-eat-dog society. Sometimes the dog at the end bites the ankle of the one in front. If you are going to do anything about the causes of crime, you have to make this a more humane place in which to live. You have to bring the community together, but not in a dog-eat-dog, free enterprise system.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, CROWN LIABILITY ACT, IMMIGRATION ACT, PAROLE ACT   JURISDICTION GIVEN TO CANADIAN COURTS TO TRY PERSONS FOR CERTAIN OFFENCES COMMITTED OUTSIDE CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Bill C-71 now before us contains a series of amendments to the Criminal Code which constitute the first stage, but a very important one, of the government legislative program. The purpose of this program is, in fact, to assure in Canadian society the mainte-
January 27, 1976

nance of the physical security climate needed for the individual and social development of Canadians. Bill C-71 includes several amendments to the Criminal Code, amendments that have not held the attention of the media until now despite their significance. Some of these concern organized crime, such as the one that makes it illegal to use for legal purposes funds obtained in an illegal manner, as well as the one that makes illegal any conspiracy in Canada to commit offences abroad.
Also to be noted are substantial changes when it comes to bail, particularly in cases of murder charges, relapse into crime or drug trafficking. These changes, Madam Speaker, are meant to ensure greater protection against those who infringe on the basic social contract by attacking the basic right to physical security of any individual living in society.
Though they may not deal with the problem of organized crime, other amendments are nevertheless aimed at improving protection of the civic right to physical integrity. Thus, very stiff penalties will be imposed for impaired driving. I hope that those penalties will be noted, that they will receive wide publicity to reduce the number of impaired driving cases. The corporal as well as material damages specifically described with the support of statistics by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), damages caused by people who have had too much to drink and insist on driving, are really excessive. I hope, Madam Speaker, that these penalties will lead to the consideration of the seriousness of this antisocial behaviour.
Finally, some amendments will protect the rights of the victim. The victim of a rape will no longer have to submit, except with the judge's authorization and in camera, to a thorough cross-examination of her background which often seemed to make her an accused rather than a victim.
Finally, the Criminal Code is amended to make sure that an acquittal by a jury can no longer be changed in a verdict of guilty by an appeal court. Indeed, I should like to mention in passing in this regard that it is obvious that when courts of appeal, whether the Quebec Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court of Canada, have in fact reversed the decision of a jury, they have been acting under an existing provision of the Criminal Code and have been in fact entitled to judge the case in question in view of the situation of the law at that time. It was up to Canadian Parliament to amend the Criminal Code. The situation at that time no longer corresponded to the needs of today's Canadian society.
I would like to come back briefly, Madam Speaker, on two or three aspects of the bill, namely the laundering of illegally obtained funds, bail provisions and drunken driving. First, let us consider the laundering of money obtained through crime: it is a well known fact-and several cases of this nature have been brought to light during the sittings of the CECO and other investigations into organized crime in Canada as well as in the United States-that organized crime is making an increasing use of illegally obtained funds, for instance, money obtained by prostitution networks, by trafficking of narcotics and drugs, by rings of motor vehicle thieves, and by something which is well known in certain areas of the south shore and Montreal, namely the protection industry. It is a well known
Criminal Code
fact that these illegally obtained funds are used to launch honest business ventures.
Under section 312 of the Criminal Code it is an offence to have in your possession an illegally obtained property. Under the amendment proposed in the House today, in future not only will the possession of illegally obtained funds be subject to prosecution under the Criminal Code, but also these funds can now be followed to their ultimate destination. This means for instance that if organized crime starts a business venture with funds obtained through the sale of stolen bonds, these funds will now be subject to the law.
The amendment goes further, and I believe it should be pointed out. It even forbids the use in Canada for legal purposes of funds obtained through underworld operations abroad. These are therefore important amendments, particularly in respect of organized crime when criminals try to lay out their illegal gains to advantage by buying commercial firms and operating legal activities.
I consider, Madam Speaker, that this is an extremely important development in Canadian jurisprudence. This is an additional tool we are giving to police forces, investigators and governments at both levels, provincial and federal, in Canada, and which will allow better control over the underworld and the mafia's sprawling operations and activities.
As to the bail, Madam Speaker, I would like to talk about it for a few moments. If there is an aspect which retains the attention of the public, it is very often indeed that of bail. Mass media do emphasize cases of people charged with an offence and who are let out on bail. We hear of it every day.
Madam Speaker, I think it is with good reason that many such cases are given prominence, particularly when the individuals released on bail commit an offence while out on parole.
In order to ensure better protection for society, Bill C-71 proposes thorough amendments to the Criminal Code as regards bail in certain specific cases.
At this moment, any person charged with a criminal offence must be let out on bail, unless the Crown attorney shows to the satisfaction of the court that the public interest requires he be imprisoned until his trial.
Bill C-71 establishes four exceptions to this principle. In these specific cases, it will be the responsibility of the defendant to show the court why he should be free pending his trial. This is therefore a reversal of the burden of proof which is very important and which should provide the public with additional protection without, however, depriving the defendant of his right to avail himself of the principles in which we all believe and, more particularly, of the principle of presumption of innocence.
In four very specific cases, it is the defendant rather than the Crown who will have to assume the burden of proof. It is the defendant who will have to prove that he is not a public danger and, secondly, that it is to be expected that he will appear before the court at the moment determined for his trial. First, when someone is charged with having committed a criminal offence while on bail, he will have to reverse the burden of proof himself. A citizen of a country other than Canada will have to do the same.

January 27, 1976
Criminal Code
In both latter cases we are dealing with amendments which were brought forward to the committee by the Minister of Justice himself (Mr. Basford). They concern charges of murder, of conspiracy to commit murder or of drug and narcotic importation or, once again, conspiracy and traffic or drug and narcotic importation.
It goes without saying that very often, particularly in the case of drug trafficking, the criminals are freed on bail and shortly after return to the street to continue this traffic of drugs which has proved so disastrous for Canadian youths in particular.
Evidently, as I have said, this does not in any manner affect the principle of our criminal law which presumes any person is innocent until proven guilty. There are nevertheless cases when, for public protection, it is necessary to ensure the presence of the accused in court. We then have to be much stricter and the present Minister of Justice as well as the Crown had no hesitation in adopting a harder line and being very strict towards the accused.
In those cases, as I have already pointed out, it will no longer be incumbent on the Crown, and this bears repeating, to prove why the accused should be held in custody until his trial, but instead, it will be up to the accused to prove why he should be free, to the satisfaction of the judge. The burden will be that much heavier.
Madam Speaker, it should also be noted in passing that the government intends to impose considerably more severe sanctions for drunken driving. Once again, inebriety at the wheel, which plagues our society, is a practice that leads, all in all, to tragedies, as well for the driver as for innocent victims, because of a lack of control or because the wheel was not taken over by someone else when too much alcohol was consumed.
Madam Speaker, I should also like to note how interesting it is that a good part of the population should be aware of the penalties now provided for by the Criminal Code for drunken driving, as a result of having been accused of driving while intoxicated, according to the rate of alcohol stipulated in the Criminal Code.
For a first offence, the maximum penalty is therefore increased. At this time, the law provides for a minimum fine of $500, or three months in prison, to a maximum fine of $2,000 or six months in prison.
For a second or third offence, there are minimum prison sentences, the judge not even having the option to impose a fine. He must sentence the person convicted to a period of detention, while for a second offence the maximum sentence is raised from three months detention to one year. And in the case of any subsequent offence, the maximum sentence is increased from one year to two years imprisonment.
Now, this clearly indicates, Madam Speaker, the interest taken by the drafters of this bill in this serious problem, and their decision in conscience to try to put an end to these abuses and emphasize the seriousness of such an act. Those are some of the amendments contained in this legislation. As I said earlier in my remarks, Madam Speaker, this is a first stage which will soon be completed by the peace and security program which the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General of Canada, I hope, will launch in the near future.

A society which is concerned with the interests of citizens must favour the establishment of a social system which meets the aspirations of its members. Daily facts demonstrate that society must take the necessary measures to isolate those who refuse to abide by the rules and that as long as it is required by public interest.
The Criminal Code is one of the instruments which allow us to settle some situations. We must always remember that that instrument of social control is used when rules are not respected. Moreover it cannot in itself contribute to reducing the derogation rate and the solution in many cases rests with other human disciplines and government programs which ensure to all Canadians a rather high minimum level in the education field and the opportunity to develop themselves and to realize their own destiny.

Madam Speaker, I just wish to make a few comments. I hope you will permit me to make them, although they are not all tied closely to the bill. I have looked for an occasion to say these things for some time. I am saying them in a personal way and expressing a personal point of view. I listened with a great deal of interest to the comments of my hon. friend from Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams); the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), and others. They were very interesting remarks of a constructive nature dealing with the causes of crime and other matters.
It seems to me that generally there is no simple approach to the question of maintaining law and order. Certainly we cannot cope with this problem by thinking simply in terms of detection and punishment. But there is no point in pretending-I am sure none of us does-that it is simply a matter of reorganizing the community, that if we had the proper spirit and took the proper precautionary measures in advance there would be no crime to contend with afterwards.
I suspect we have to attack crime on many fronts. For example, there is a vast difference between highly organized crime on the one hand and the kind of crime which reflects slum conditions, poverty, and so on. I would myself welcome the kind of inquiry which many speakers inside the House have called for, an inquiry into the causes of crime, an inquiry into the effects of violence on television, among other things. As I say, I suspect we have to attack the problem on many fronts, and although many of us have hobby horses we like to ride, none of them, perhaps, would take us very far by themselves.
My hon. friend from Calgary North attacked the idea of minimal and mandatory sentences in connection with breathalyzer convictions. I agree with him 100 per cent. I cannot understand why the government would sponsor minimal or mandatory sentences in connection with something like this. Generally, I express disapproval of the whole idea of a minimum sentence, so what I am going to say with regard to breathalyzer tests is in no way derogatory to or divergent from the view expressed by my hon. friend. However, I will make one point with regard to
January 27, 1976

breathalyzer tests and related matters such as the mandatory requirement to wear seat belts and the attitude some people seem to take that it is a requirement which somehow infringes their personal liberty.
Their attitude seems to be that it is somehow an infringement of personal liberty for parliament to pass a bill requiring a person to wear a seat belt or to take a breathalyzer test.
