I have no God-given right to drive a car on a highway; that is a privilege granted me by the province or state. Any legislature or the Parliament of Canada has a perfect right, indeed a duty, to impose safeguards and precautions upon me while I am driving on the highway. I am not the only one who drives on the highway; others do, too. I have no God-given right, either, even if I were alone on the highway, to drive in any way I please or to do any damage to myself or the car.
I simply say as fervently as I can that I believe our legislatures and this parliament have a heavy obligation to improve safety on our highways and to cut down carnage. I do not want to be intolerant, but I have very little time for anybody who argues that they have a right to refuse to take a breathalyzer test if stopped on the highway and asked to do so, that somehow this is an infringement of peronal liberties. If people want to drive a car on the highway, then they have to be prepared to accept and comply with measures considered by legislatures and by parliament to be necessary. I have no right to drive a car without using a seat belt if the legislature of my province or if the Parliament of Canada, if it were within the jurisdiction of parliament, require me to do so. As I say, Madam Speaker, my rights are not being infringed; I am exercising a privilege.
In view of the amount of carnage being done by people on the highway, when I was in provincial politics and premier of a province I felt that we should take very tough positions to reduce the damage taking place on our highways. I do not intend to stay in public life very long, and this is one reason I have seized upon this opportunity this afternoon to express as strongly as I can my deep personal conviction that some people, at least, seem to be confusing a privilege to drive on the highway, a privilege granted by the state, with some God-given fundamental right that never existed.
I hope that parliamentarians and legislators will pursue this course of being tough with people who violate the laws and rules governing the conduct of motor vehicles on the highway. I think we have taken far too lax a view of the consequence of things like speeding and careless driving. I want to tell the minister that I will give him my full support for being as tough as he wants to be toward people driving while impaired and toward imposing reasonable methods of picking these people up-and if it happens to be me, that is too bad.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had to address myself to some elements of Bill C-20 and to my concerns with regard to this bill. Although I can see some advantages flowing from it, there are also some very serious concerns. My principal concerns relate to qualifications for citizenship, qualifications that are deemed to be of a very serious nature. It is a very solemn undertaking indeed to accept not only the benefits of citizenship but the responsibilities that must inevitably accompany the privilege of being a Canadian.
This bill would permit a person to qualify for citizenship on the basis of allowing every day spent in Canada to qualify as a half day prior to being registered as a person lawfully in Canada. I think that is a gross error. Certainly, with my knowledge of the facile way that people can move across the border between Canada and the United States, this has to be an error. With my knowledge of the sloppy manner in which some people have been admitted to Canada, it is an error.
I recall a young lady who, as a part-time employee of customs and immigration, made a suggestion to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) in 1974 to the effect that people coming to Canada through various border crossing points, claiming they were landed immigrants, should be able to provide some form of official identification issued by the ministry. This identification should take the form perhaps of a plasticized identification card giving a description of the person to whom it was issued, together with a recent photograph. We are asked to provide that sort of thing when we apply for a passport. Indeed, every member of the House of Commons has this kind of identification.
This very valid suggestion was passed to the minister and accepted by him, but like so many other suggestions that are made to some ministers, that was the last we heard of it, even though the minister himself endorsed this very concept in writing. As it stands now, we have no idea how long a person has been in Canada prior to the period when they begin to qualify for citizenship on the basis of a full day in Canada equalling a full day in their application for citizenship.
This brings me to the next provision in clause 5, that for every day during which the applicant was resident in

January 27, 1976
Citizenship
Canada after his lawful admission in Canada he shall be deemed to have accumulated one day of residence. That is for a period of three years, Madam Speaker. According to the bill, he shall be conversant with at least one of the official languages. He should have a knowledge of Canada, and not only a knowledge of Canada but an understanding of Canada. I submit it is one thing to have a knowledge of Canada, and another thing to have an understanding of Canada and the manner in which this country, our people and our governments operate.
On the basis of my experience with citizenship judges, I must say that some have demonstrated a lack of knowledge of the very basic concerns of Canadians. This is often brought to light at the time these people make application for citizenship. I know there are those in this House and in this country who feel a person after three years should qualify for citizenship. I also know in my own riding, where I have a very wonderful cross-section of people of various ethnic origins, that the value they place on Canadian citizenship, something they have worked for and earned, is much in excess of the token three years that this bill provides. I almost get the feeling that this is sort of a citizenship for sale or bargain day agreement. Let us make it easy, open the borders and allow them to pour in!
I do not think for one minute that a person has to express any bias or that there should be any implication of being labelled a bigot or a racist when you suggest that the regulation remain as it is with a five-year qualification for citizenship. Certainly we have those who have never adapted to Canadian citizenship or to Canada. I suggest to hon. members that three years is indeed a very brief time in order to reap the rewards of Canadian citizenship, and that five years is a much more acceptable standard and one that is easily appreciated and understood by a cross-section of Canada's ethnic groups.
There are certain provisions for the loss of citizenship, and certain provisions for those who may have lost their citizenship to regain that valuable status. With reference to clause 7, I wonder just who is going to advise the person who has reached the age of 28 years that it is now time to apply for that status for which he should have applied earlier. What happens to the fellow who has not been informed? Are we looking at some broad-brush advertising scheme to be conducted once a year by Manpower and Immigration just to assure that this man or woman is fully aware of the regulation?
It is bad enough for most of us to try to keep track of all the regulations from day to day, without this kind of nonsense being inserted in the bill. I cannot really see the merit or the value of it. I think provisions for Canadians are well covered in other areas of the bill and I see no need for this particular provision.
Thank heavens, however, that the minister in his wisdom has decided that those women who were British subjects prior to 1947 can now, on application to the minister, obtain a certificate. There are no more outspoken people in the matter of their right to vote and their Canadian citizenship than those British who by virtue of previous legislation were, quite frankly, denied their right to vote. Of course, it is easy to say that they never applied

for citizenship, but in every other context they have considered themselves to be Canadians. They have considered themselves to be proud Canadians and British subjects who have contributed to the economy of this country by paying taxes and in every other way doing their jobs. I am relieved at least that clause 3 of this bill will make this provision, particularly for women, who are the most outspoken of those who are very proud to be Canadian citizens. I suggest it will be incumbent upon the Minister of Manpower and Immigration to give this part the widest possible publication.
It will be incumbent upon members of parliament to let their constituents know precisely the facts of this particular provision so these people can apply. Many times these British subjects have spoken to me, saying that if that be the case and they cannot vote without having applied for Canadian citizenship, they surely will not vote. In some respects that is an unfortunate attitude, but in other ways, in view of the contribution these people have made to the community, I cannot really blame them.
When we get to the question of examination for citizenship, then, Madam Speaker, the weaknesses of the system are becoming in fact more apparent. One of my concerns is that there is lack of uniformity by citizenship judges in dealing with applicants. This lack of uniformity, leaving it up to the individual citizenship judge, is going to be very seriously compounded by the three-year provision.
Not too long ago I listened to the complaints of several applicants for citizenship who appeared before a judge in my riding. Can you imagine the question being put, to somebody from Iran applying for Canadian citizenship, who had examined, studied and learned to speak one of our official languages and tried to become part of the fabric of Canada, having resided here for the qualifying period in excess of five years: "What can you tell me about white faces?" If he had asked me, I would not have been able to provide the answer, as I am sure very few members in this House could.
This judge asked: "What can you tell me about white faces", and that is the way he put the question. If he had said: "Can you tell me about white faces", I might have said: "You are talking about cattle, or Herefords." I could tell him something about Hereford cattle. But what in the world could we expect a man from Iran to know about white faces? I am sure the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Hurlburt) would have been hard pressed to figure out what that judge was talking about, and he should know if anyone should.
Another applicant was asked to talk about the pre-Cambrian shield. I think that is very important to the student of geology, or possibly to the student of geography, but just how relevant is it to a requirement for citizenship in Canada? These are only two of several examinations where applicants for citizenship have really, in effect, been put down by the examining judge. That is why I ask, if these people are having difficulty in five years in responding to the questions of this judge to whom I referred-and how many other citizenship judges across Canada are asking similar questions-how many problems are they going to find generated by the three-year provision? Are we going to have a different style of questioning? Is it to be primarily textbook questioning, or are we really going to deter-
January 27, 1976

mine that these people truly sense what is Canadian and have some knowledge about what is Canada?
Madam Speaker, I simply cannot accept the basic premise or idea that citizenship is for sale at bargain prices and for bargain requirements. I am also concerned about the requirements for citizenship and the discretionary power to the governor in council or the minister with reference to refugees. We are indeed fortunate in Canada that we live in a democracy and that to all intents and purposes, save and except for the ever-increasing, burgeoning government legislation, we are as free as we are and do not live in a police state. When a minister has the discretionary power to examine the applications of refugees or those who claim refugee status, it is so easy for a minister to say he really cannot conceive how that person should feel he or she can be a refugee from such a fine country as Poland, or such a fine country as Hungary or any other iron curtain country. I know whereof I speak, Madam Speaker.
I know, Madam Speaker, that very shortly I will be making an appeal to the minister. May I say, also, that I have made a recommendation to the minister that you should have a cabinet post. Perhaps my message will get through to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I think there would probably be unanimous consent if the question could be put to a vote.
To continue, very shortly I expect I will be approaching the Minister of Manpower and Immigration with reference to the problem of persons who claim refugee status. I am sure this same problem has been confronted by more than one member of parliament. I really do not think that, as Canadians, we have fully grasped the total loss of freedom there is in the police type of state that exists behind the iron curtain and the satellite countries. I do not think we understand the situation in respect of a woman who reaches age 65. Such a woman is old long before her time, she is bent and torn and is no longer of any value to the state. She is a person who must be clothed, kept warm and fed.
We do not seem to understand that these are the people who are granted exit visas to visit Canada and the United States or any other country in the free world. However, in the case of an attempt to obtain an exit visa for some young, productive worker, whether male or female, then a different connotation is put on the application. I would ask members to observe the manner in which persons from behind the iron curtain are handed their visas when they line up to receive them. If they are being granted a visa to visit one of the western countries, they find that when their visa is being presented to them it is thrown to the floor so that the applicant must bend down to pick it up.
If I, as a Canadian, report to the police in Budapest or at some other place while I am entering or leaving as an alien, that is different. Then my visa or passport is handed to me. If I should be a worker contributing to the economy of that particular country, and should apply for a visa to leave that country, even for a short visit to relatives in another country, then my application is treated with a great deal of disdain and there is a great deal of discouragement.
How many young people from the iron curtain countries do we see in Canada as visitors? The answer is, damned
Citizenship
few. When such a visitor wishes to stay, what assistance are we prepared to give? When such a person must return to his or her country, what consideration is truly given to the application to remain in Canada? Do we believe that these people have no problems when they return to the police state behind the iron curtain and that they will be accepted with open arms? If we do, how very naive we are.
It is not my intention to protract the debate on this citizenship bill, because there are some advantages for some people. I realize the government is anxious to see it pass. However, I must protest strongly the bargain rates for citizenship and join many Canadians of all ethnic origins who say they want to work for their citizenship, that they are prepared to work for it and do not mind the five years. They feel that is a short enough period in which to gain the values and the benefits and respond to the requirements of being a Canadian. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker, for the opportunity to address you on this bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am naturally quite pleased to take part in this debate since for several years I have had the honour of introducing in the House some bills dealing with amendments to the Citizenship Act. I was therefore happy when the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) introduced Bill C-20 dealing with amendments demanded for a long time by the members as well by various groups other than French or English in Canada, unfortunately called ethnic groups. Indeed, it is a well-known fact that I dislike that term; I prefer the term "future new Canadians" or "prospective new Canadians." There is in this legislation, and I refer to clause 5, a clause I am very much interested in, since for some four years I have called for such changes, asking the government to reduce from five to three years the required period to hold permanent residence in Canada before getting or applying for Canadian citizenship. I wish to thank my colleagues and the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) for having listened to my arguments and now to submit them for study to the House and committees in order to enact the new Canadian citizenship legislation. Canadians who had been accepted-I should rather refer to them as future new Canadians-to become landed immigrants will certainly be extremely happy, as soon as this legislation is passed, to send their application to become Canadian citizens after three instead of five years.
I could never really understand why in a country where communications are so fast, where it is so easy for everyone to have a full knowledge of our institutions, why then, one had to wait for more than five years to become a Canadian citizen. I submit Madam Speaker, that a three year waiting period is quite sufficient for those who have decided to get a Canadian citizenship.
And I am glad that we will soon have this new designation. I am very careful and I regret that my friend the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) is not here now. In fact, when I talk about British citizen and Commonwealth citizen I know that this matter interests him very much and that he always listens very carefully. I wish to tell him through the chair that I am glad that soon in our Canadian passports, if this citizenship legislation is passed, we will replace the words "a Canadian citizen is a British subject" by "a Canadian citizen is a member of the Commonwealth". I think that it will enhance our Commonwealth status to have in our passports the words "Member of the Commonwealth" rather than "British citizen" with all due respect to those who in another country are called British citizens. It is something I wish to emphasize.
Of course, I would have been glad had this government found advisable, at clauses 40 and 2 concerning oaths of allegiance, to follow the Canadian constitutional trend and change the oath of allegiance. For those who could be very sensitive and nervous I repeat that I can live with this bill, that I will accept it as it is but I wish to say to this House that I would prefer that all new citizens take an oath of allegiance to Canadian institutions which, once again, could be helpful to those who now refuse to take the Canadian citizenship because they think they are taking an oath of allegiance to the head of another country when everybody knows that the Queen, who is the Queen of England, is also the Queen of Canada. But I hope that some day, some of my colleagues opposite wherever they are
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
sitting at that time, when I will be older, will themselves propose that change. However, I wished to say that I would have preferred to see that change in the new Citizenship Act.
Madam Speaker, I wish to make some further comments. I think it was time for this legislation to provide equality of rights for men and women. This is so elementary, so logical that I do not see any reason why I should waste the valuable time of this House trying to show how these amendments to the Citizenship Act are justified.
Of course, I am also pleased that soon our youth-
-those for whom under the bill the age of majority is reduced from 21 to 18, the age of federal enfranchisement.

Of course, Madam Speaker, it was logical I think that our young Canadians now be able to exercize their right to vote at the age of 18, that they enjoy such freedom and that, even if their parents decide otherwise, they have the privilege of asking for Canadian citizenship.
I therefore congratulate the minister for his wisdom and for listening to us-but there again I do not want to get involved in any partisanship. Representations were made by both sides of this House. However, I must say that since I have been interested in this matter for many years, I made such representations to different ministers and when I was Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State, I had even advocated making such changes, to which the minister had agreed. I now realize that this government is determined to increase these means to provide our citizens with further services, which I will explain, Madam Speaker, since it is important that our friends in the press- [English]
These people are the ones who will give great publicity to this new immigration law or citizenship law or any new laws at great length, so that Canadians will learn about these changes.

Here is one of those changes, Madam Speaker. The minister has allowed the citizenship bureaus to remain open evenings and Saturdays. Unfortunately, the fact is not well known, but I hope the new aspiring Canadian citizens, who are excellent workers, and who often hesitate to take three days off of their precious time to go and apply for citizenship, can thus be better served, for in many cases, the employers refuse to give them a day off to file their application for citizenship, another to appear before the citizenship judge and still another to take the oath of allegiance required to become a Canadian citizen. Facilities will be provided for by the government at its offices in Toronto and Montreal and, I hope, in Vancouver and elsewhere in due course, where there is need for them. Naturally, during a time of austerity, offices should not be opened everywhere, and new aspiring citizens should take advantage of the great number of services already available to them.
I should also like to echo what my hon. colleague across the way, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco)
January 27, 1976

said when he spoke of the sensitivity with which the citizenship judges should deal with the applicants.

The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) spoke about the question put by a citizenship judge to a man from Iran: "what do you know about white faces?". I also know a judge who had the temerity, if I may put it that way, to ask a future new Canadian of Italian origin, "what would you do if Canada ever declared war on Italy?" I do not think such a question should ever be asked because it is unfair. We know that the man would probably answer that he would fight for Canada, but I think it is the most unfair question one could put to a future Canadian citizen because never, in my recollection, has any judge ever asked of the hundreds of thousands of excellent British citizens who came from Great Britain what they would do if Canada ever declared war on Great Britain. So I believe that if such a question is never asked of a British citizen it should not be asked of citizens of other countries of origin.
This is a very sensitive matter. This was an English speaking judge in Quebec, and it happened recently. I am speaking in English, but in case I do not say exactly what I want to say it is because I am talking about "la sensibilite" and I do not know how to translate that word.

But I hope that judges will have that necessary compassion when examining witnesses. And since many of my colleagues wish to speak on this subject, I would like to conclude by asking whether the government would not accept amendments in committee on such a possibility. I had requested it and I make a further request today in this House. For a number of years now I have been making representations concerning very old citizens who speak neither English nor French, but whose children are Canadian citizens or applied for and were granted citizenship many years ago. These elder citizens live in a so-called ghetto, without any pejorative connotation. Being quite old they cannot speak either English or French, since they came to Canada at the request of their children now enjoying an adequate economic status allowing them to come to Canada to spend here the latter part of their lives. I wonder if it would not come within the scope of the policy of compassion which the government should apply at all times when dealing human beings if it were to give the Court of citizenship the power to grant citizenship almost automatically to parents and grand-parents of Canadian citizens, even though they may not speak English or French or have a very precise knowledge of Canada. Anyway, when I see questions put to new citizens, I always wonder how many Canadian-born citizens could pass such an examination, and what would be their marks. I am not referring here to members in this House, because I know that members from all sides, whether Social Credit, NDP, Progressive Conservative or Liberal, would pass the exam. But still I wonder if, from time to time, we would not hesitate before providing the answers to all the questions that are put to potential citizens.
It is a question of allowing latitude to the judges. I know that the great majority of them do have the sensitivity needed, this ability to recognize that Canadian citizenship must not be granted to whomever wants it without at least having confirmation that the applicant does intend to be
Citizenship
an excellent Canadian. But it is always good to let those who are entrusted with its final administration, our officials whom I congratulate because I see them at work in the various offices, improve on the process. There is always room for improvement as much in the case of members of Parliament and, naturally, high officials as for lower echelon officials but I congratulate them because generally speaking they carry out their work with excellence and sincerity. Then there remains the question of allowing some latitude to judges. They could best exercice this their latitude if they were allowed to grant citizenship to people at a certain age, perhaps 70, but I would favor 65. Citizenship would be granted to those people who often have been in Canada for 15, 20 years and who will die without ever having the opportunity to learn French or English. Needless to say that I join my colleague the hon. member for Kootenay-West in the wishes he made.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CONDITIONS AND PROVISIONS GOVERNING CITIZENSHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to be very brief with my remarks respecting Bill C-20, as I know there are one or two others who would like to speak before six o'clock.
I am in favour of this bill in general principle as indeed I believe are most members. I like the idea of the waiting period for citizenship being reduced from five years to three years. This move is long overdue and I welcome it.
The age of majority will be reduced from 21 years to 18 years. This is a logical step because the age of majority for Canadian citizens in all provinces I believe, and certainly federally, is 18 years.
Men and women are finally to be treated equally. It was a sad commentary on the old Citizenship Act that they were not. Now, for example, children born abroad will derive citizenship from either parent. At the present time a child acquires Canadian citizenship only if the father is Canadian.
Another example is that all applicants for Canadian citizenship will be required to meet the three year residence qualification without regard to marital connection with a citizen. Under the present act only one year of residence is required for the alien wife of a Canadian citizen. The act is certainly bringing into reality in law what has been the actual practice and I am happy about those changes.
British subjects will no longer be exempt from the requirement to be examined by a citizenship judge or to attend a citizenship ceremony. I happen to be only half Canadian as my father was born in England. In my constituency there are a lot of persons of Anglo-Saxon background who are touchy about the fact that some of their traditional so-called rights are being infringed upon. I say frankly, openly, and honestly that I do not know why we should continue giving any special exemption to immigrants from the United Kingdom when those same rights are not given to immigrants from other countries. I am prepared to meet criticism from people of Anglo-Saxon origin in my constituency, and I think this bill is fair to all ethnic groups entering the country.

January 27, 1976
Citizenship
The removal of the discrimination against women is certainly in line with the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. This has been long in coming but I am happy that it has finally arrived in Bill C-20.
The reduction in the eligibility age makes sense since the voting age is now 18. Some people have argued that this provision should have been introduced under the Elections Act. That is a moot point which I will not belabour. In effect this changes things after the fact and this argument has been made previously.
The period of residence required prior to application for citizenship is another important change. It seems obvious that the present five year wait was an arbitrary decision, as indeed is the proposed three year wait. I do not know how we would arrive at the correct figure, whether it be one year, two, three, four, or five, but certainly the reduction is a step in the right direction.
The five year period was probably imposed because very often the wives of immigrants who stayed home to raise their families did not get out into the work force, or out of the home, and so found it difficult to pick up the language. I do not think this should be an obstacle. In cases that I am familiar with, the wives do try their best to communicate, particularly those from eastern Europe or the Mediterranean countries from where most of our immigrants now come. If their children are learning English or French and their husbands are speaking English or French, I do not think they should be held back.
I should like to deal briefly with the powers of the minister. The new act will take many of the burdens off the minister's back, such as the direct responsibility for granting citizenship. However, as my colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), stated, under clause 18 of the bill the governor in council may still intervene in the granting of citizenship in cases where a person is thought to be a threat to Canada or "contrary to the public order in Canada". The declaration by the governor in council will be conclusive. I suppose under these circumstances we must have some final authority which can decide whether a person should be granted citizenship. It seems somewhat of an anomaly, however, that on the one hand the bill purportedly takes away final authority from the minister for granting citizenship but leaves the door open for the governor in council to deny it. This point should be given further consideration. Last spring I was involved in fighting to have a certain undesirable individual deported from this country but he is still residing in Montreal. I still think that there should be a right of appeal, which should extend even beyond the final analysis of the governor in council.
Clause 5(l)(b)(i) is vague and needs clarifying. It reads:
for every day during which he-
He being the person who is a prospective citizen here on a minister's permit.
-was resident in Canada before his lawful admission to Canada for permanent residence he shall be deemed to have accumulated one-half day of residence.

In other words, someone here on a ministerial permit for one year can count six months towards his or her three years requirement for citizenship. The justification for this escapes me. When this bill was debated earlier the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), to justify clause 5( 1)(b)(i), mentioned an example. He said that say a woman aged 62 comes to Canada as a tourist and then decides to stay. It could take years for her to obtain landed status, but those years would, by way of clause 5(1)(b)(i), not be wasted. I submit that such a justification discriminates against those who are not yet in Canada.
If somebody comes over to visit a relative, say, on a three-months visitor's visa, and has it extended to six months, nine months, 12 months

they go up to as much as 15 months, even two years-that visitor can apply time in Canada toward the three year residency requirement. People can short cut the waiting period that way. Why should not people waiting in their home country be entitled to time for waiting? I suggest that the present provision would encourage people to try to enter this country by the back door approach, as it were. I think the minister should explain this provision fully. As I say, it discriminates against those who are not yet in Canada. That is an important point.
People who are prepared to wait in Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom, or states in Africa and go through regular channels are being penalized. They must wait the full time. On the other hand, those who come in as visitors and remain on a visitor's visa for three months, six months or one year are entitled to have their days in this country included in the waiting period. The logic of that provision escapes me.
I will not take much more time. Generally speaking, I am in favour of the bill. Let me make one more point and then I will sit down. Clause 33 of the bill has been referred to, and it reads in part:
Real and personal property of every description may be taken, acquired, held and disposed of by a person who is not a Canadian citizen in the same manner in all respects as by a Canadian citizen ...
Obviously this clause does nothing to alleviate the concerns of some provinces, especially Maritime provinces, with regard to foreign ownership of land. The problem is that if provinces act on their own to curtail non-citizen land ownership, will they not be in conflict with this federal law? The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) said in the House on May 21, 1975, that very interesting legal interpretations and court cases could arise whereby non-citizens challenge provincial laws, using federal statutes to back up their case. As other hon. members have said, it will be interesting to see how the minister deals with this question. I hope the minister will clarify the points I raised.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am deeply concerned that this bill, which includes provisions for the equal treatment of men and women in the matter of citizenship, has been delayed before the House for such a long time. We have heard members of the opposition give their endorsement to many major provisions of the bill, including those which provide for the equal treatment of men and women. Nevertheless while the bill remains before the House those very provisions which have been applauded cannot be put into practice. I had personally
January 27, 1976

hoped that this bill would be passed during 1975, International Women's Year, the year in which Canada, with other United Nations member countries, undertook to encourage equal treatment, equal opportunity, and equal responsibilities for women and men in all aspects of our society. This bill is central to the provision of equality for women in Canada.
The report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women was tabled in 1970. It included the following recommendation regarding the Canadian Citizenship Act:
... that sections 4 and 5 of the Canadian Citizenship Act be amended to provide that a child born outside Canada is a natural-born Canadian if either of his parents is a Canadian citizen.
Clause 3(1)(b) of Bill C-20 implements that recommendation. It says that a person is a citizen if:
... he was born outside Canada after the coming into force of this act and at the time of birth one of his parents, other than a parent who adopted him, was a citizen;
There has been some debate about whether this provision should be retroactive to cover those children who have been affected by the present Canadian Citizenship Act which does not include this provision. However, it is felt that there are real dangers in granting citizenship retroactively. I am happy to say that the advisory council on the status of women agrees with Bill C-20's treatment of this point. Two other of the royal commission's recommendations were:
... that either citizen-parent may apply for the naturalized citizenship of a minor child ... that, in the case of joint adoption, the child may be granted Canadian citizenship if either of the adopting parents is a Canadian citizen.
Bill C-20 also implements these recommendations. Clause 5(2) provides that:
The minister shall grant citizenship to any person who, not being a citizen, has been lawfully admitted to Canada for permanent residence and is the minor child of a citizen if an application for citizenship is made to the minister by a person authorized by regulation to make the application on behalf of the child.
This will in many cases cover the problem mentioned earlier stemming from the fact that the bill is not retroactive. As long as the child is living in Canada a Canadian mother will be able to obtain citizenship for a child born before this bill becomes law.
Another recommendation of the royal commission reads:
. . . that the Canadian Citizenship Act be amended so that there is no difference between the requirements for the acquisition of Canadian citizenship by an alien husband and an alien wife of a Canadian citizen.
With the passage of this bill this discrimination will disappear entirely. There will be no claim to citizenship through marriage for either spouse. Spouses of either sex will have to fulfil the ordinary residence requirements.
Finally, the royal commission recommended:
... that the Canadian Citizenship Act be amended to provide for the automatic resumption of Canadian citizenship by women who lost it because they married aliens before January 1,1947.
The bill before the House provides in clause 10(2) for the automatic resumption of citizenship for such women, on writen notice being given to the minister that they elect to be a citizen. The bill does not make this resumption retroactive since it was considered that, to do so, could have an adverse effect upon those women for whom the
Adjournment
automatic conferring of Canadian citizenship without their knowledge could create difficulties.
The bill now before the House includes the provision that a woman who lost Canadian citizenship by marrying an alien before January 1, 1947, can now apply for and receive citizenship immediately as a matter of right, simply on giving notice to the minister. In this way women affected by the pre-1947 law can receive citizenship automatically but it will not be retroactively conferred on them without their knowledge. This bill then, Madam Speaker, deals with five substantial and central recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. In fact with the passage of this bill one of the major obstacles to equal treatment of women and men under federal law will be removed.
